hints: Think about when the chromatid pairs (each chromosome made of two sister chromatids) first get organised into a neat line in the middle of the cell.
Then think about when those sister chromatids are actually pulled apart to opposite ends, so each side gets exactly one copy.
walkthrough:
**Remember the job of mitosis**

Think of it like sharing out identical twins fairly. Each chromosome after S phase has two identical sister chromatids joined together. For repair, each daughter cell must get one chromatid from every pair.

So we need a line-up step plus a pull-apart step.

**Line up in the middle - metaphase**

In metaphase, all the chromosomes line up on the metaphase plate (the equator). Spindle fibres attach to the centromere from opposite poles.

This perfect lining up makes sure one chromatid faces one pole and its sister faces the other pole.

**Pull apart to opposite poles - anaphase**

In anaphase, the centromere divides and spindle fibres shorten. The sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles as daughter chromosomes.

This is the moment each future daughter cell is guaranteed one copy from each pair, so B is the answer.

options.A: Prophase only condenses chromosomes and breaks down the nuclear envelope, it does not line them up or separate chromatids.
options.B: Metaphase lines up each chromatid pair on the equator, and anaphase separates sister chromatids to opposite poles, giving identical sets.
options.C: Anaphase does separate chromatids, but telophase only reforms nuclei around the already separated sets, it does not do the lining up.
options.D: Telophase and interphase do not line up or separate chromatids. Interphase is not even part of mitosis, it is DNA replication and growth.
